The ηinv and mechanical power loss (Pl,mech) were experimentally measured, as shown in Fig. 10. The inverter used
in this study comprises an electronic speed controller for
BLDC motor controlled using pulse with modulation (PWM)
method and a motor driver that control the power and speed
of the motor by adjusting the duty cycle of the PWM signal.

The ηinv is affected by the loss due to the internal resistance
of the inverter and the loss due to field effect transistor (FET)
switching. In this study, assuming that the ηinv is a function
of rotational speed [27], the ηinv was measured by operating
the pump under no-load condition without a working fluid.
The ηinv was calculated by dividing the inverter output power
by the input power. The ηinv was measured to vary depending on the rotational speed, current, and voltage. At very
low rotational speeds of less than 10,000 RPM, there was
significant difference in ηinv depending on the voltage. However, the change in the ηinv depending on the voltage was
not considered because the voltage was fixed in the study.
Moreover, since the ηinv converged to approximately 80%
for both the current and rotational speed used in the test, the
ηinv was assumed as 80%. The Pl,mech is power loss due to
friction between the shaft of the pump and the bearings and
seals, which is proportional to the rotational speed. Pl,mech
was calculated by measuring the power consumed by the
motor under no-load condition and the inverter output power
under no-load condition was divided by the ηmotor.

As shown in Fig. 11, post-processing of the steady state
data was performed using a kernel filter with a rate of 50 Hz
and a filter sample size of 51. The yellow area in Fig. 11
means a steady-state area after the flow is stabilized at the
test target rotational speed. The mean value of the data in the
yellow area was used as the test result.

**4.1** **Cold-Water Test**

In this section, the affinity laws for pumps with a constant
impeller diameter are verified using the test results. In addition, by comparing the numerical and theoretical analysis
results with the test results, the reliability of the numerical
and theoretical analyses was evaluated. Finally, the hydraulic
performance of the pump with type A and type B impellers
was compared by estimating the performance at the design
point based on a theoretical analysis.

**Fig. 13** Performance curve derived by affinity law with 18,000 RPM
data of type B impeller

**4.1.1** **Hydraulic Performance**

Figure 12 shows the theoretically developed pressure based
on the above head loss model and the cold-water hydraulic
performance test data. The head loss model was validated
by comparing the test data and theoretical value. The trends
of the performance curves of both values are similar, but
there are some differences in the values. The friction loss
increases with increasing flow rate, while the slippage loss,
shock loss, and leakage loss increase with decreasing flow
rate, Therefore, the difference between the theoretical value
and experimental value increases at the low flow rate because
the actual values of slippage loss, shock loss, and leakage loss
were smaller than the calculation. However, considering that
the measurement error of rotational speed in the experimental
environment was ± 5%, the head loss model was consistent
with the test data. Figure 13 shows the test data and performance curves calculated using the affinity law based on the
test data with a rotational speed of 18,000 RPM. The affinity
law was verified by comparing the test data and the values
calculated using the affinity law.
